section.title: Glorious Things of Zion
section.sectionRationale: A short song of the sons of Korah, this psalm celebrates Zion as the city God founded and loves, then astonishes by declaring that former enemy nations will be registered as citizens born in Zion, a vision of the church gathered from every people that is fulfilled in Christ and pictured in the heavenly Jerusalem.
section.thesis: God has founded Zion and loves her above every other dwelling, and He will one day register even Israel's ancient enemies as citizens born within her, a promise of worldwide inclusion fulfilled in the church, made citizens of the heavenly Jerusalem through Christ.
section.frameNote: Three movements: Zion's secure foundation and God's special love for her, verses 1-3; the astonishing registration of the nations as citizens of Zion, verses 4-6; and the joyful song of those who find every spring of joy in God, verse 7.

units.label: God's City on the Holy Mountains

verses.text: He has {{yasad|founded}} His city on the holy mountains.
The LORD loves the gates of Zion more than all the dwellings of Jacob.
Glorious things are ascribed to you, O city of God. Selah

units.label: This One Was Born in Zion

verses.text: I will mention Rahab and Babylon among those who know Me, along with Philistia, Tyre, and Cush, when I say, 'This one was {{yalad|born}} in Zion.'
And it will be said of Zion: 'This one and that one were born in her, and the Most High Himself will establish her.'
The LORD will record in the register of the peoples: 'This one was born in Zion.' Selah
Singers and pipers will proclaim, 'All my {{mayan|springs}} of joy are in You.'

yasad.gloss: To found, to establish securely. God Himself, not human builders, has founded Zion on the holy mountains, giving her an unshakeable foundation.

yalad.gloss: To bear, to give birth. Used here of former enemy nations being registered as though born in Zion, picturing a new spiritual birthright and citizenship granted by God's own decree.

mayan.gloss: A spring or fountain of water. The psalm's closing image pictures every source of joy and life as flowing from God alone, the true spring behind the city of God.

basic.context: This short song of the sons of Korah celebrates Zion, the city God founded and loves above every other place in Israel. It then makes an astonishing claim: nations that were once Israel's enemies, Egypt, Babylon, Philistia, Tyre, and Cush, will one day be registered by God Himself as citizens born in Zion.
basic.hermeneutics: The psalm describes Zion's unique historical status as the place of God's presence, and it prescribes an abiding hope: God's plan always included the nations, a hope that becomes reality in the worldwide, multiethnic people gathered into Christ's church.
basic.originalLanguages: God has yasad, founded, His city, verse 1, and the psalm pictures foreign peoples as yalad, born, in Zion, verses 4-6, a spiritual birthright granted by divine decree. The closing verse rejoices that every mayan, spring or fountain, of joy is found in God alone, verse 7.
basic.typology: Zion, the city of God's presence, points forward to the heavenly Jerusalem, the true and lasting city of God to which believers from every nation have already come. The registration of foreign nations as native-born citizens anticipates Gentiles being made fellow citizens with the saints in Christ.
basic.christ: Christ builds His church out of every nation and tongue, fulfilling this psalm's vision that former strangers to God's covenant would be registered as citizens born in Zion. Through faith in Him, believers are no longer strangers and aliens but fellow citizens with the saints and members of the household of God.
basic.god: God is shown as the founder of Zion who loves this city above all others, and as the sovereign King who personally registers citizens from every nation, including former enemies, granting them full standing in His city by His own gracious decree.
basic.crossReferences: Ephesians 2:12-19 pictures Gentiles, once strangers to the covenants of promise, made fellow citizens with the saints. Galatians 4:26 calls the Jerusalem above our mother. Hebrews 12:22-24 describes believers as having already come to Mount Zion, the city of the living God.
basic.oneStory: This psalm's vision of Zion as the city God founded and loves, and of former enemy nations registered as her citizens, finds its fulfillment in Christ's church, gathered from every nation and already, even now, citizens of the heavenly Jerusalem.

context.literary:
Psalm 87 is among the most compressed poems in the Psalter, only seven verses, and the Hebrew is so terse that translators disagree about several lines. Its design is a widening circle. It begins with a place, the holy mountains, verse 1. It moves to a people, the gates of Zion and the dwellings of Jacob, verse 2. Then in the centre it opens to the world, naming five nations, verse 4. The last verses fold the circle back again to Zion and to a song, verses 5 to 7.

The middle section rests on a refrain. 'This one was born in Zion' appears in verse 4 and again in verse 6, and verse 5 says 'this one and that one were born in her.' Three times the same sentence is spoken over a foreign name. The repetition is like the repeated calling of a roll. A second structural signal is the word Selah, which closes verse 3 and verse 6, marking a pause after the city's glory and another after the registering of the peoples. The psalm is thus divided into a stanza about the city, a stanza about the nations, and a short closing line of song.

The form is a Song of Zion, the same family as Psalms 46, 48 and 76. Those psalms describe the city as a fortress that cannot be shaken. Psalm 87 is unusual because it never mentions a siege or an enemy attack. The enemies are not fought off; they are enrolled. The psalm is speech in God's voice, in verse 4 and verse 6 especially, so that the astonishing promise is not the speaker's wish but God's own declaration.
context.historical:
The five nations named in verse 4 were not random. Rahab, the BSB footnote explains, is a poetic name for Egypt. Babylon was the great power of the east. Philistia was the old enemy on Israel's coast. Tyre was the trading city to the north, and Cush, the footnote says, means the upper Nile region, far to the south. Together they cover the compass: south and south west in Egypt and Cush, west in Philistia and Tyre, east in Babylon. They are the peoples Israel knew from history as oppressors, rivals and distant strangers.

The title of the psalm belongs to the sons of Korah, a family of Levites who served as gatekeepers and singers. A gatekeeper's attention to who belongs inside the city and who does not would make the image of a register natural to them. They loved the house of God, as Psalm 84 also shows, and they knew its gates.

Some interpreters connect the psalm to a time when God's city had been delivered from danger, such as the rescue of Jerusalem in the days of Hezekiah, and others to the time of exile when Jerusalem lay in ruins. The psalm itself gives no date. What it does give is the first hearers' sense of Zion as a city chosen by God, in a world where every other capital was built on human power. A register in which foreign peoples are recorded as natives would have been a scandal, since citizenship in the ancient world rested on birth and blood. The psalm uses the language of birth to say that entrance into God's city rests on His word, not on ancestry.
context.canonical:
The psalm sits between two very different neighbours. Psalm 86 ends with an individual's prayer that the nations will bow, and Psalm 88 plunges into the darkest lament of the Psalter. Psalm 87 is the burst of light between them, and its placement teaches that the darkness is not the last word. Both Psalm 87 and Psalm 88 belong to the sons of Korah, which binds the joy and the sorrow together in one family's hymnal.

The idea that the nations will share in Zion runs through the prophets. Isaiah sees the nations streaming to the mountain of the LORD, Isaiah 2:2 to 3, and foreigners joining themselves to the LORD finding a place in His house, Isaiah 56:6 to 7. Isaiah 19:24 to 25 names Egypt and Assyria together with Israel, and the LORD says 'Blessed be Egypt My people, Assyria My handiwork, and Israel My inheritance.' Psalm 68:31 pictures Cush stretching out her hands to God. Psalm 87 brings these strands to a point: the nations are not just visitors but citizens by birth.

The image of a register has a long history. Names are written in a book in Exodus 32:32, Psalm 69:28 and Isaiah 4:3. In the New Testament the register becomes heaven's roll. Jesus told His disciples to rejoice that their names were written in heaven, Luke 10:20. Hebrews 12:22 to 23 says believers have come to Mount Zion, to the heavenly Jerusalem, the congregation of the firstborn enrolled in heaven. Paul says the Jerusalem above is our mother, Galatians 4:26, and that our citizenship is in heaven, Philippians 3:20. Revelation completes the picture with the nations walking by the light of the city, and only those written in the Lamb's Book of Life entering it, Revelation 21:24 to 27.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The sons of Korah wrote this for people who lived inside a fragile, small nation and who would naturally measure the world by Israel's borders. They meant to stretch that measure. They begin where any Israelite would be comfortable, with the city of God loved above all the dwellings of Jacob, and then they stun the reader by putting Egypt and Babylon, Israel's old oppressors, on the same register as native sons.

The point is not that Zion is less special. The point is that Zion is special precisely because the God who founded it is the God of all peoples, so that to be born in Zion is to be born into His family. The hearers are meant to adopt a new imagination: to look at the nations around them and see not only threats but future citizens.

The psalm also means to shift attention from the human builders of the city to its divine Founder. The Most High Himself will establish her, verse 5, and the LORD Himself will write the names, verse 6. The hearers are to put their trust in God's action, not in their own achievement. The closing picture of musicians declaring that all their springs are in God shows what kind of community this is: one whose source of life and joy is found in Him alone.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The psalm describes what God declares He will do; it is a promise, not a command. Nothing in it tells Israel to go and register the nations, and nothing in it tells believers that they earn citizenship by their own efforts. The registering is God's own act, verse 6. A careful reader should not turn the promise into a plan for human engineering of the church.

What does carry forward is the attitude the promise is meant to produce. A community that believes God intends to write former enemies into His register cannot treat those enemies as beyond hope. The New Testament draws exactly this conclusion, as when Paul tells Gentile believers that they are no longer strangers but fellow citizens, Ephesians 2:19. The psalm also does not erase the particular gift to Jacob, for verse 2 still says the LORD loves the gates of Zion. A reader should hold the two together: God's particular love of Zion and His purpose to widen the circle of her children.

debates.question: Who are the people who are 'born in Zion' in verses 4 to 6?

views.label: Gentile converts from the named nations
views.case: The text lists Rahab, Babylon, Philistia, Tyre and Cush as nations and says God will mention them 'among those who know Me.' The natural sense is that individuals from these nations come to know the LORD and are counted as natives of His city. This is how the New Testament reads the vision, Ephesians 2:19 and Galatians 4:26.

views.label: Jews living in those lands
views.case: Some take the register as a roll of Israelites scattered in Egypt, Babylon and other countries, each claiming Zion as his birthplace or spiritual home. On this reading the psalm celebrates the diaspora's bond with the city. The text does not say these are Israelites, however, and the list of names fits enemy nations better than exiles.

debates.bearing: The text's plain sense favours the nations. The New Testament confirms it, making the psalm a foundation text for the inclusion of the Gentiles. Even the second view would still be a testimony to Zion's wide reach.

debates.question: What does verse 7 mean by 'All my springs are in You'?

views.label: A song of the joyful citizens of Zion
views.case: The BSB supplies 'of joy,' reading the springs as sources of gladness. The singers and pipers are the newly registered citizens, and their song says their whole life is nourished by God. This reading fits the festive picture of a city in worship.

views.label: A reference to the water of Zion or the source of life
views.case: The Hebrew is brief, and some see a reference to the river and springs of the city of God, as in Psalm 46:4. The springs would then describe the source of blessing that flows from God's presence to the people, without any special stress on joy.

debates.bearing: Either way the song says that the source of the city's life is God Himself. The BSB's 'joy' is an interpretive addition, but it fits the mood of the psalm. The verse's line is best held loosely, since the Hebrew is difficult.

study.originalLanguages:
Five details of the Hebrew help the psalm come alive.

The first is the word for 'register' in verse 6. The phrase 'record in the register of the peoples' uses the verb for writing, and the picture is the written roll of a people. Elsewhere Scripture speaks of being 'recorded among the living' in Jerusalem, Isaiah 4:3, and of a book from which names can be blotted out, Exodus 32:32 and Psalm 69:28. The psalm applies a familiar image of covenant membership to foreigners.

The second is the verb 'mention' in verse 4, in the sense of calling to remembrance. God speaks the names of the nations aloud in a positive, personal way, as when a teacher reads a class list. The word has nothing to do with their past enmity. The word 'among those who know Me' pairs with it, since 'knowing' the LORD in the Old Testament is covenant intimacy, not mere acquaintance, as in Jeremiah 31:34.

The third is the name Rahab. In other places Rahab names a mythical sea monster that God crushed, Psalm 89:10 and Isaiah 51:9. Here the BSB footnote says it is a poetic name for Egypt. The psalm thus takes a word used for chaos and defeat and lets it stand among the ones who know the LORD. The same word appears in the very next psalm but one, Psalm 89:10, in its older sense, so the reader meets both uses within a few pages.

The fourth is the expression 'the Most High,' Elyon, in verse 5. It is the title for God as ruler over all nations, used in Deuteronomy 32:8 of the God who apportioned the peoples. The psalm uses it at exactly the moment the nations are being admitted, because the God who gave them their places is the God who now grants them a new birth.

The fifth is the word Selah at the end of verses 3 and 6. Its meaning is uncertain, though most take it as a musical or liturgical pause. Whatever it meant, it marks two turning points, after the glory of the city and after the registration of the nations.

Finally the last verse is so terse that translators differ on it. The Hebrew is very short, and the BSB fills it out with the words 'will proclaim' and 'of joy.' The brevity is itself a clue to the psalm's style: it gives the reader much more than it explains.

typology.type: Zion, the city God founded, Psalm 87:1
typology.fulfillment: Zion on its holy mountain stood for the place where God dwelt with His people. The writer to the Hebrews takes the image and tells believers 'you have come to Mount Zion, to the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem,' Hebrews 12:22. The earthly city was a shadow; the heavenly city is the substance, and it cannot be shaken, Hebrews 12:28. Paul adds that 'the Jerusalem above is free, and she is our mother,' Galatians 4:26. The type falls short because Jerusalem's walls could be, and were, broken down, while the city to come is founded by God and has foundations, Hebrews 11:10.

The psalm speaks of birth to describe entry into God's city. Jesus uses the same language when He tells Nicodemus that no one can see the kingdom of God unless he is born again, John 3:3, and Peter says believers have been born again through the living word, 1 Peter 1:23. What the psalm pictured as a divine decree over the nations, the New Testament shows as the new birth. The correspondence is real, but the psalm says nothing of how the birth comes about, which the gospel supplies in the cross and the gift of the Spirit.

typology.type: The register of the peoples, Psalm 87:6
typology.fulfillment: The register of the nations points to the Lamb's Book of Life. Jesus told His followers to rejoice that their names were written in heaven, Luke 10:20, and Revelation says the nations enter the city, but only those whose names are written in the Lamb's book, Revelation 21:24 to 27. The type finds its escalation in a book that belongs to the Lamb who was slain. Where the psalm is silent about what secures a name in the register, the New Testament says the Lamb's blood does.

study.christ:
The psalm leads to Christ by its central promise: that people from every nation would be counted as native born in God's city. Paul says plainly how this happened. Gentiles were once 'foreigners and strangers,' but now, in Christ, are 'fellow citizens with the saints and members of God's household,' Ephesians 2:19. He says that Christ 'made the two one' and broke down the dividing wall of hostility, Ephesians 2:14. The enemies the psalm names, Egypt and Babylon, are the ones whose descendants have been received. What the psalm proclaimed in God's voice, the cross accomplished.

It leads to Christ by the picture of the city. In Hebrews the believer has already come to Mount Zion, to the congregation of the firstborn enrolled in heaven, Hebrews 12:22 to 23. Jesus is named in the same passage as the mediator of a new covenant, Hebrews 12:24. The firstborn of the psalm's imagery is His title, for He is 'the firstborn from the dead,' Revelation 1:5, and 'the firstborn over all creation,' Colossians 1:15. To be registered in Zion is to be placed in a family whose elder brother is Christ, who 'is not ashamed to call them brothers,' Hebrews 2:11.

It leads to Christ by the way citizenship is secured. The psalm says God Himself writes the names, and the New Testament says the register is the Lamb's Book of Life, Revelation 21:27. A citizenship granted to former enemies has to be paid for, and Paul says the price was Christ's blood, which brought near those who were far off, Ephesians 2:13. Jesus's own words at the end of His ministry point in the same direction: 'I have other sheep that are not of this fold,' John 10:16, and 'when I am lifted up from the earth, I will draw all people to Myself,' John 12:32.

It leads to Christ by the song of the last verse. The springs of joy are found in Him. Jesus told the woman at the well that the water He gives would become in the believer a spring of water welling up to eternal life, John 4:14, and on the last day of the feast He cried out that anyone who is thirsty should come to Him and drink, John 7:37. The singers who said 'All my springs are in You' spoke better than they knew.

A caution is in order. The psalm does not mention a Messiah, and it would be wrong to read Jesus into each line. The honest link is one of promise and fulfillment: what the psalm pictures as God's act in Zion, the New Testament shows as God's act in Christ.
study.god:
The psalm shows God as a Founder. He has laid the foundation of His city on the holy mountains, verse 1, and the Most High Himself will establish her, verse 5. The Hebrew verb for 'founded' is the word used for laying a building's base, and it carries the thought of a work that will stand. Zion does not rest on the strength of Israel's armies or the wisdom of its kings. It rests on God's choice and God's work, which is why the psalm can speak of her glory without any note of self congratulation.

It shows God as one who loves particular things. 'The LORD loves the gates of Zion more than all the dwellings of Jacob,' verse 2. God is not vague in His affection; He chooses, and His choice is a sign of grace, not of merit. This is a needed correction for any doctrine of God that makes Him a remote principle. The God of this psalm has a city He loves.

It shows a God whose love is not bounded by the borders of that city. The same God who loves Zion speaks the names of Egypt, Babylon, Philistia, Tyre and Cush, and says of each person from those nations, 'This one was born in Zion.' The text does not hide the astonishing kindness of this. The nations were Israel's enemies, yet they are declared family. God's holiness and His welcome are not in tension here. The city is holy, and the city is open.

It shows God as the one who keeps the register. He mentions, He records, He establishes. The action words of the psalm, in verses 4 to 6, all have God as their subject. Human beings do not apply for citizenship; they are declared citizens. This teaches the sovereignty of grace in its gentlest form, and it guards worship from any pride: if God wrote the name, no one can boast.

And it shows a God who is the source of joy. The last verse's singers confess that all their springs are in Him. Worship in this psalm is neither duty nor performance but the natural song of people who have found where life comes from. The God of this psalm is worthy of praise because He has done the building, the loving, the welcoming and the writing, and the only fitting response is a song.

crossReferences.note: All nations stream to the mountain of the LORD's house to be taught His ways. The vision is the prophetic counterpart to Psalm 87:4 to 6, where the nations are counted as born in Zion. Both texts picture Zion as the centre to which the world is drawn by God's own work.

Egypt and Assyria are named together with Israel, and God calls Egypt 'My people' and Assyria 'My handiwork.' The prophet here names the very sort of enemy nations the psalm lists, and gives them the titles once reserved for Israel. The two passages read together show the same astonishing promise.

Envoys come from Egypt and Cush stretches out her hands to God. Cush and Egypt appear again in Psalm 87:4, which suggests the psalmists shared a hope that these distant peoples would turn to the LORD. The earlier psalm sees them coming; the later one says they are registered as natives.

Foreigners who join themselves to the LORD are brought to His holy mountain, and His house is called a house of prayer for all peoples. This is the prophetic basis for the psalm's welcome of outsiders, and Jesus quotes it in the temple, Mark 11:17.

Jesus tells the seventy-two not to rejoice that spirits submit to them but that their names are written in heaven. The same register image as Psalm 87:6 becomes the ground of a believer's joy, the assurance that God Himself has recorded the name.

Paul's phrase sets the heavenly city over against the earthly one, and the psalm's idea of being born in Zion is given a New Testament form: believers are children of the heavenly city, born by promise and not by ancestry or effort.

Gentiles are no longer foreigners and strangers but fellow citizens with the saints and members of God's household. This is the psalm's promise in apostolic words, including the language of citizenship and family. Paul grounds it in the cross, Ephesians 2:13 to 16.

Believers have already come to Mount Zion, the heavenly Jerusalem, and to the congregation of the firstborn enrolled in heaven. The writer sees the psalm's city and register as present realities for those who belong to Christ, though the full display is yet to come.

The nations walk by the light of the city and the kings of the earth bring their glory into it, but only those whose names are in the Lamb's Book of Life enter. The psalm's register of the peoples reaches its final form.

study.oneStory:
Psalm 87 answers a question that hangs over the first eleven chapters of Genesis and the story that follows. After Babel scattered the nations, Genesis 11:8 to 9, where do the nations belong? The psalm says that in the end they belong in Zion. The scattering is not final, and the peoples who were divided by language and pride are to be gathered into one city by God's own decree.

It also answers the tension of the Abrahamic promise. God said to Abraham that through his offspring all nations of the earth would be blessed, Genesis 22:18. Yet through much of the Old Testament the nations appear as enemies, Egypt that enslaved, Babylon that destroyed, Philistia that raided, Tyre that traded and Cush that stood distant. Psalm 87 says that the blessing promised to the nations is not only to be received at a distance. It is to be received as birth in the city of God.

Looking forward, the psalm sets up the work of Christ and the mission of the church. The Gospels end with the command to make disciples of all nations, Matthew 28:19. Acts shows the gospel crossing from Jerusalem to Samaria to the ends of the earth, Acts 1:8, and the Ethiopian, a man of the region of Cush, is among the first foreigners to be baptised, Acts 8:26 to 39. The letters describe the dividing wall as broken down, Ephesians 2:14, and Hebrews says believers have already come to the heavenly Jerusalem, Hebrews 12:22.

The story ends in the city itself. In Revelation the holy city comes down from heaven, the nations walk by its light, and the kings of the earth bring their glory into it, Revelation 21:2 and 24. Those who enter are those whose names are written in the Lamb's Book of Life, Revelation 21:27. John also sees a great multitude from every nation, tribe, people and language standing before the throne, Revelation 7:9. The psalm's short, startling register is the seed of that vast assembly, and every name God has mentioned will be there.

quiz.q: According to verse 1, who founded the city of Zion?

options.text: God Himself, on the holy mountains.
options.note: The psalm opens by attributing Zion's foundation directly to God, not to human builders.

options.text: King David alone, by his own military strength.
options.note: David did historically capture the stronghold of Zion, but this psalm credits the city's deeper, true foundation to God Himself, not merely to David's conquest.

options.text: The Philistines.
options.note: The Philistines are named among the nations later drawn to Zion, not as its founders.

options.text: No one; the city arose by chance.
options.note: The psalm is explicit that God founded the city with purpose.

quiz.q: What astonishing declaration is made about the nations in verses 4-6?

options.text: That nations once hostile to Israel, like Egypt and Babylon, will be registered as citizens born in Zion.
options.note: This is the psalm's central surprise, that former enemies would gain full citizenship by God's decree.

options.text: That these nations will be permanently destroyed.
options.note: The passage announces their inclusion as citizens, not their destruction.

options.text: That Israel will conquer and enslave these nations.
options.note: The vision is one of gracious inclusion, not conquest or enslavement.

options.text: That these nations, once hostile to Israel, will change their relationship to God.
options.note: This is true in a general sense, but the specific declaration in verses 4-6 goes further: they will be registered as citizens actually born in Zion.

quiz.q: What does verse 7 identify as the source of all joy?

options.text: God Himself; 'all my springs of joy are in You.'
options.note: The closing verse locates every source of joy in God alone.

options.text: The wealth of the city of Zion.
options.note: The psalm points beyond material wealth to God Himself as the source of joy.

options.text: Military victory over enemy nations.
options.note: The psalm's tone toward the nations is inclusion, not celebration of conquest.

options.text: The city of Zion itself.
options.note: Zion is closely connected to this joy, but verse 7 specifically locates the true source of joy in God Himself, not the city as such.

quiz.q: How does the New Testament fulfill this psalm's vision of nations registered as citizens of Zion?

options.text: Gentiles are made fellow citizens with the saints and members of God's household through Christ.
options.note: Ephesians 2:12-19 describes exactly this fulfillment, former strangers now full citizens through Christ.

options.text: It has no fulfillment in the New Testament.
options.note: Paul directly applies this theme of Gentile inclusion in Ephesians 2.

options.text: It is fulfilled only by the physical rebuilding of Jerusalem's walls.
options.note: The fulfillment is spiritual citizenship through Christ, not merely physical construction.

options.text: It is fulfilled as Gentile believers come to worship the true God through Christ.
options.note: This is true and closely related, though the fullest New Testament expression, Ephesians 2:12-19, speaks specifically of fellow citizenship, not merely general worship.

quiz.q: What does the register kept by the LORD in verse 6 signify?

options.text: God's own personal, authoritative record of who belongs to His city.
options.note: The verse pictures God Himself, not human officials, keeping this register of citizenship.

options.text: A census for taxation purposes only.
options.note: The register is about spiritual citizenship and belonging, not merely civic taxation.

options.text: A list of Israel's enemies to be destroyed.
options.note: The register lists those counted as belonging to Zion, not enemies marked for destruction.

options.text: A record affirming true spiritual citizenship and belonging.
options.note: This is close to correct, but slightly understates that the register is specifically God's own personal, authoritative decree, as verse 6 emphasizes.

questions: This psalm celebrates that God Himself founded and loves Zion. Where do you find your own sense of belonging and security, and does it rest on something as sure as God's own foundation?
Verses 4-6 declare that God would register former enemy nations as citizens of Zion. Is there a person or group you find hard to imagine welcomed fully into God's family?
The psalm pictures citizenship in Zion as granted by God's own decree, not earned. How does knowing your standing before God rests on His declaration, not your effort, change how you approach Him?
Verse 7 says all springs of joy are found in God. Where have you been seeking joy from a source other than God this week?
Believers today are citizens of the heavenly Jerusalem, Hebrews 12:22. How should that heavenly citizenship shape the way you view your earthly circumstances and loyalties?

translationNotes.note: Literally the Hebrew reads His foundation is on the holy mountains, a construction the BSB renders as He has founded His city for clarity.
Rahab is a poetic name for Egypt, and Cush refers to the upper Nile region, so the four named peoples together span the compass around Israel.
This one was born in Zion functions as a formula of legal registration, granting foreign individuals the same standing as native-born citizens.
